title: Sanford Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Sanford wells have a 120-foot median depth, with finished well costs commonly estimated at $12,000-$21,000.
h1: Sanford, Colorado Well Depths, Yields and Costs
intro_html:
If you are buying land or a home near Sanford, the local well records give a useful starting point: the median reported well depth is 120 feet, and the middle half runs from 100 to 200 feet. Reported yields are also generally strong, with a 15.0 gallon-per-minute median among the wells that list a pump yield.

These records cover permitted wells within 5 miles of Sanford in Conejos County. They are planning information, not a guarantee for a particular parcel. The actual result depends on the lot, aquifer, well construction, water rights, and the driller’s findings during construction.

sections.heading: Sanford well depths reflect shallow local conditions, with exceptions
sections.html:
Sanford’s median well depth is 120 feet, and the middle half of reported wells falls between 100 and 200 feet. That is a practical range to use when asking for a preliminary drilling estimate. The depth mix shows that 25% are under 100 feet, while 59% fall from 100 to 300 feet.

There are important exceptions. The 90th-percentile depth is 433 feet, 8% of wells are between 300 and 600 feet, and another 8% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record reaches 2,000 feet. Permits identify both unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer conditions and the Confined San Luis Valley aquifer system, so nearby results should guide expectations without replacing a site-specific bid.

sections.heading: Most Sanford wells report useful production, but test the actual lot
sections.html:
Only 104 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are not a test of every permitted well. Among those reports, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-two percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 36% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute.

Low-producing wells are present but uncommon in this dataset: 2% are under 1 gallon per minute and 1% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. A buyer should still request the well construction report and pumping information. Household demand, storage, irrigation, livestock, and any water-rights limits are separate questions from the well’s measured yield.

sections.heading: Sanford water levels are shallow, with a small decade-to-decade change
sections.html:
The median static water level is 5 feet below the ground surface, and the middle half ranges from 0 to 11 feet. That indicates shallow water levels in many reported Sanford-area wells, but it does not mean every parcel will encounter water at the same depth. Ground elevation, well location, aquifer, and measurement conditions matter.

The decade summaries show a median of 2 feet below surface for measurements in the 2010s and 6 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper reported median in the newer decade, but the records do not by themselves establish a long-term regional decline. Ask for the original static water level, pumping level, and date of measurement for any existing well you are considering.

sections.heading: Sanford’s permit history shows long local drilling experience
sections.html:
Sanford-area permit records extend from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. The records include 1,126 permitted wells, with 873 recorded as constructed. Permit activity was highest in the 1970s with 188 permits, followed by 178 in the 2000s, 167 in the 2010s, and 110 in the 2020s.

The most active drillers listed in these records are Rocky Mountain Waterworks LLC (Phythian, Donald L.) with 100 wells, Martin, Gale with 46, and Heersink Drilling (Heersink, Scott) with 41. Those names show who appears frequently in the record, not who is available or best for your parcel. Verify current licensing, insurance, references, casing and grout practices, and the scope of the written proposal.

sections.heading: A typical Sanford well budget starts with depth, then adds the system
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described in the local cost model, a typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At Sanford’s 120-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $6,000 to $9,000. That is not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,000 to $21,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing requirements, unusual water conditions, or longer utility runs can move the final price outside that range. Get the bid to identify included footage, casing, grout, development, pump sizing, pressure equipment, electrical work, trenching, testing, and permits. Compare bids on the same scope rather than on drilling rate alone.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole risk, septic space, and building access
sections.html:
The mapped environmental information is favorable in one respect: there are 0 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. That does not prove water from an individual well is safe. Test an existing or new well for the contaminants relevant to the property and confirm the results with the appropriate local authorities.

There are 16 historic mine features in the same broader area, so location-specific review still matters. Low-yield and dry-hole risk cannot be ruled out from a median alone, especially where fractured-bedrock conditions are involved. Before building, confirm well access for a rig, a suitable septic area, separation from the well, driveway grades, utility routes, and the water rights needed for the intended use. New household-use wells may also require compliance with Colorado DWR permit conditions and, in over-appropriated basins, an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: Use nearby wells to investigate a Sanford lot before closing
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s DWR permit and construction report, then compare wells near the property rather than relying only on the area median. La Jara is about 3 miles away, Manassa about 6 miles, Romeo about 8 miles, and Capulin about 11 miles; those areas can provide context, but the closest comparable wells are more useful than a distant average.

For an existing home, confirm the well’s permit status, construction, static and pumping levels, yield test, water quality, storage, pressure, and repair history. For vacant land, ask a licensed driller for a written site review and a cost range based on nearby depths and aquifer conditions. Keep a contingency for a deeper-than-median hole, and make sure the proposed well, septic system, access road, and building envelope work together before you commit.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Sanford, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported Sanford-area well is 120 feet deep, and the middle half runs from 100 to 200 feet. However, 8% of wells are 300 to 600 feet and 8% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record is 2,000 feet, so nearby well records should guide a parcel-specific estimate.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Sanford, Colorado?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 120-foot median depth, drilling alone is estimated at $6,000 to $9,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,000 to $21,000.

faq.q: How much water do Sanford wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 104 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 12.0 to 15.0. Sixty-two percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. The figures do not guarantee a new well, so request a pumping test and review the construction report.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Sanford?
faq.a: Records show 0 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but that is not a drinking-water guarantee. Test the individual well. Also review its construction, nearby septic systems, historic mine features, and the contaminants recommended for the property.

faq.q: Are Sanford water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The median reported static water level was 2 feet below surface for measurements in the 2010s and 6 feet in the 2020s. That indicates a deeper median in the newer decade, but the available series does not prove a continuing regional decline. Check the individual well’s dated static and pumping levels before buying.
